title: MESA: Task-Adaptive Multi-Structure Evidence Selection for Long-Horizon Agent Memory

visual_explainer.blocker: Two isolated GPT Image attempts on 2026-08-13 failed paper-specific Visual QA: the first rendered an unrelated GitHub repository dashboard with fabricated maintenance metadata; the second rendered a V-Mem explainer instead of MESA. Binary publication is available; the blocker is render grounding/paper identity.

analysis.tldr: MESA treats memory access as structure-level composition: construct several complementary views once, then learn an explicit query-adaptive policy that selects a subset rather than always reading one view or all views.
analysis.problem: Multi-structure memories face a read-time trade-off: a fixed union adds redundant/noisy evidence and token cost, while route-to-one prevents complementary global, temporal, relational, semantic, and step-level evidence from being combined.
analysis.core_idea: Build five fixed views of each trajectory—summary, temporal store, knowledge graph, vector database, and raw episodic trace—then optimize an inspectable selection policy from answer-level feedback. For each query the policy selects a non-empty subset, invokes each view's native access operator, composes the returned evidence, and passes it to a frozen answer model.

memory_design.write: Offline builders convert each trajectory into five complementary memory structures; builders remain fixed while the selector is optimized.
memory_design.organize: Maintain summary, temporal, graph, vector, and raw episodic views as complementary representations rather than collapsing them into one store.
memory_design.read: An explicit query/context-conditioned policy selects a subset of structures; their native retrievers return evidence that is composed before a frozen answer model.
memory_design.update_forget: The evaluated structures are fixed after construction. MESA evolves the access-selection policy, not the stored memories; continuous update and forgetting are not studied.

compared_to: AMA-Agent and other long-horizon memory baselines
Reading all five structures for every query
Routing each query to exactly one structure
analysis.evidence: On AMA-Bench with Qwen3-32B, MESA reaches 65.1±0.8% overall accuracy versus 56.6% for AMA-Agent. The diagnostic comparison is selection: route-to-one scores 57.0%, all five structures 63.7% with 18.7k evidence tokens/query, while MESA selects 2.8 structures on average and reaches 65.1% with 11.0k tokens—1.4 points above all-structure with 41.2% fewer evidence tokens. A domain-conditioned fixed policy already reaches 64.4%, so the gain from fine-grained learned selection over a strong coarse selector is modest. On LoCoMo, MESA reports 49.0 F1 versus 47.2 for EMem.
analysis.why_it_matters: This strengthens a more precise design rule than 'use multiple memories': structure is useful when the access layer can choose which relations to expose for the current decision. The negative comparison to both route-to-one and read-everything makes the composition boundary the real contribution.
limitations: The library is limited to five preselected structures, so the result does not establish which representation set is optimal.
A validation-selected domain-conditioned policy reaches 64.4% versus MESA's 65.1%, so some gains can be explained by coarse query/task regularities.
Constructing all complementary views adds offline cost relative to simpler systems even though read-time evidence is reduced.
Continuously updated and multimodal memories are not evaluated, and builders/retrievers are not jointly optimized with the selector.
